item.title: AI helps learning more when it is used to understand than when it does the task
item.description: A review by Stanford University now brings together 52 studies measuring the effect of AI on learning: using it to understand new material fares better than using it to produce the work, although no use improves results consistently. This report explains how to read those studies, why a tutor that asks questions is not enough on its own and what a teacher can do so that AI does not do the students’ work.

media:content.media:description: Infographic: a student facing an AI assistant with two paths. At the top, “Hand in”: the AI does the work and, without the tool, the result falls: “Without the tool: −17%”. Below, “Understand”: the assistant asks questions and the student corrects their own errors: “64% self-corrected”. Underneath, four recommendations: “Try it first”, “Tutor asks”, “Split the tasks” and “Check without AI”.

item.title: Gemini Notebook now has an official API, though limited and in preview
item.description: It lets other programs create notebooks and add sources to them, but only with personal accounts. An unofficial code library does more, although it may stop working without warning.

media:content.media:description: A diagram of two paths to the same notebook: the upper one, labelled “Official API”, passes through a padlock and carries the label “Personal only”; the lower one, labelled “Unofficial”, is a dashed red line with the label “May break”. On the right, the notebook, labelled “Notebook”.

item.title: An Argentine handbook brings the environmental, labour and social costs of AI into the classroom
item.description: Two researchers propose that secondary school teachers ask what for, from where and with what consequences artificial intelligence is used, before deciding how. The 2026 handbook takes a Latin American and feminist perspective.

media:content.media:description: Layered diagram: a screen labelled “AI assistant” rests on three stacked layers, “Decisions”, “Data centres” and “Labelling”, while a magnifying glass descends through them beside a red arrow and the question “With what consequences?”.

item.title: The image model that drew a nine-sided shape with eleven sides has been replaced in Gemini
item.description: In November 2025, Google’s new image model got some polygons right and others wrong. In February 2026 Nano Banana 2 replaced it in Gemini, and for developers there is another that costs a quarter as much per 1K image.

media:content.media:description: Diptych split by a vertical line. On the left, “Nov. 2025”: four ink-coloured banknotes and below them “$0.134”. On the right, “Today”: a single blue banknote, a quarter as many, and below it “$0.0336”.

item.title: Google DeepMind offers, in English, an interactive guide that uses its Gemma 4 model to explain how a…
item.description: Google DeepMind offers, in English, an interactive guide that uses its Gemma 4 model to explain how a language model, the kind of program behind ChatGPT, generates from a text the fragment that comes next. It goes through five stages, from splitting the text to the chat format.

item.title: The Council of the EU approves conclusions on citizens’ AI skills
item.description: Member states back the idea that people of all ages should learn to use artificial intelligence critically and responsibly. These are policy guidelines, not a rule that binds schools.

media:content.media:description: A diagram of three steps joined by arrows: a building with columns, “European framework”; a flag, “Each state”; and an open book, “Classrooms”. The dotted red arrow between the last two is labelled “Guidance only”.

item.title: Chicago weighs its options if Google withdraws search from districts that reject its AI
item.description: According to the Chicago Sun-Times, Google warns that school districts that do not allow its AI tools will lose access to search next year.

media:content.media:description: A building, “District”, with an arrow labelled “Rejects AI” pointing to a magnifying glass crossed out with a red circle, “Search”, and below it the question “No access?”.

item.title: From 9% to 36% in research-level physics: AI still fails almost two in three
item.description: In November 2025 a new evaluation of unseen physics problems was launched, and no AI model reached 10%. A year later, the best result is close to 36%.

media:content.media:description: Diptych in two halves. On the left, labelled “Nov. 2025”, a sheet with three physics challenges, all three crossed out, and the label “Fails almost everything”. On the right, labelled “Today”, the same sheet with the first challenge solved, with a blue mark, and the other two still crossed out, with the label “Still fails a lot”.

item.title: Gemini will separate conversation history from permission to train models
item.description: Google will replace the “Keep Activity” setting with two: one for history and, separately, one that lets its models use the content of conversations.

media:content.media:description: A switch labelled “Keep Activity” splits, with two arrows, into two independent settings: “History”, with a calendar and a switch, and “Training”, with a cogwheel and another switch.

item.title: Canada launches a national AI literacy initiative with three strands: students, teachers and the public
item.description: The Canadian government has launched, with the Amii institute, a national AI literacy initiative with three training strands, one of them yet to launch. The document shared in the library presents it and points out its shortcomings.

media:content.media:description: Diagram: a box on the left, “AI literacy”, from which three paths lead, each with an icon: a graduation cap labelled “Students”, a whiteboard labelled “Teachers” and a group of people labelled “Citizens”; beneath the last one, a dashed line labelled “Yet to launch”.

item.title: The 1994 Clark–Kozma debate helps in reading Stanford’s studies on AI
item.description: An academic argument over whether technology influences learning or only the method matters, recalled in the group in connection with Stanford’s review.

media:content.media:description: A drawing divided into two halves. On the left, a package labelled “Method” on a lorry labelled “Medium”, with the name “Clark”: the medium only carries the method. On the right, two overlapping circles, with the name “Kozma”: medium and method cannot be separated.

item.title: A teacher reflective journal with AI raises the question of whether the assistant supports or replaces judgement
item.description: A master’s thesis project proposes dictating after each class and having an assistant organise the text and return questions; the group debates whether that weakens judgement.

media:content.media:description: A microphone labelled “Dictation” leads to a document labelled “Summary” and to a speech bubble with a question mark labelled “Questions”. An arrow goes down from the document to a box labelled “The teacher decides”.

item.title: Free ChatGPT for teachers only in the US: a year on, the border remains
item.description: In November 2025, OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teachers and Spanish teachers wondered whether it would reach them. A year on, it has grown in US schools, but it has not crossed the ocean.

media:content.media:description: Diptych. On the left, “Nov. 2025”: a globe with a single pin on “US” and a closed padlock below. On the right, “Today”: the same globe with three blue pins on “US” and the padlock still closed, next to the label “Spain”.

item.title: Stanford gathers 52 causal studies on AI in schools and sees uneven results
item.description: The November review goes from 20 to 52 studies and concludes that AI looks more promising for understanding new material than for producing assignments, but no use improves learning consistently.

media:content.media:description: Diagram: a person uses an assistant, from which two paths lead: one towards “Understand” and another, in red, towards “Do the task”, and at the end a balance. Labels: Assistant, Understand, Do the task, Uneven.

item.title: Galicia’s parliament passes the law regulating phones, screens and AI in classrooms
item.description: The Digital Education Law limits individual use of devices up to the fifth year of primary school and was passed with the votes of the PPdeG and the opposition of the BNG and the PSdeG.

media:content.media:description: Diagram: a parliament building leads to a law, from which come a phone crossed out in red and a video camera. Labels: Parliament, Digital law, Phones, No recording.

item.title: Madrid adds to EducaMadrid an AI agent that prepares personalised materials
item.description: According to the Community of Madrid, the agent was developed by civil servants in its regional digital ministry and can be used by teachers in publicly funded schools.

media:content.media:description: Diagram: a teacher uses an agent, from which three results come: a document, a tick and an envelope. Labels: Teacher, Agent, Notes, Quizzes, Emails.

item.title: Experiment with 400 adults finds a Socratic AI tutor teaches more than explaining the mistake
item.description: Carnegie Mellon researchers compare four ways of giving feedback after a mistake and suggest that what works is sending the student back to the task until they get it right.

media:content.media:description: Two paths after a mistake, marked with a red cross. At the top, the mistake leads to a box labelled “Explanation” and from there to the next problems. At the bottom, the mistake leads to “Question”, then to “Retry”, with an arrow returning from “Retry” to “Question” until the answer is right, and finally to a tick under the label “Success”. Above, the label “64%”.

item.title: Google is rolling out temporary threads in AI Mode in its search engine: the questions in those…
item.description: Google is rolling out temporary threads in AI Mode in its search engine: the questions in those conversations are not saved in the history or used for personalisation, according to its announcement of 17 November.

item.title: Gemini Notebook turns a notebook’s sources into an interactive website
item.description: All it takes is typing “make me a site” in the notebook’s chat. Members of the groups have already tried it, and one has uploaded the result to Moodle.

media:content.media:description: Diagram from left to right: three documents labelled “Sources” go into a notebook with a chat bubble labelled “make me a site”; out of it comes a web page with a panel and lines of text, labelled “Website”, which is downloaded as a “.html” file and uploaded to “Moodle”.

item.title: Scholar Labs goes from a waiting list and English only to opening up in every language
item.description: In November 2025, Scholar Labs accepted questions only in English and many people had to join a waiting list. Since June 2026 it has been open to every signed-in user and accepts questions in all languages.

media:content.media:description: Diptych split by a vertical line. On the left, “Nov. 2025”: a closed padlock with the labels “Waiting list” and “English only”. On the right, “Today”: an open padlock, in blue, with the label “All languages” and the translation icon.

item.title: South Korea will check all glasses at the university entrance exam (Suneung) after the top scorer in the…
item.description: South Korea will check all glasses at the university entrance exam (Suneung) after the top scorer in the tax accountant exam confessed to using a micro-camera and generative AI to cheat. According to The Next Web, more than 500,000 students sit the exam at 1,300 centres.

item.title: INTEF updates its guide to AI in education with ten ethical principles and a phased plan for schools to adopt it
item.description: Version 2.0 of the Ministry of Education's guide, published in September 2026, organises the use of AI around three profiles (students, teachers and schools) and adds annexes ready for the classroom.

media:content.media:description: Three cards, each with a human figure, labelled “Students”, “Teachers” and “School”, resting on a base labelled “Three profiles”; above the school card a seven-step staircase labelled “Seven phases” rises to a circle with a review arrow.

item.title: Failed for studying from flawed ChatGPT notes; today Catalonia has 45 guidelines on use
item.description: In November 2025, a Catalan teacher said he had failed students who studied from flawed notes made with ChatGPT, and the group called for literacy and rules. A year later, the Departament d’Educació has set out how AI should enter schools.

media:content.media:description: Diptych split by a vertical line. On the left, “Nov. 2025”: a document crossed out with an X, labelled “Flawed notes”. On the right, “Today”: the same document marked with a blue check mark, labelled “45 guidelines”.

item.title: Declaring AI use: a teacher asks schools to clarify which uses are acceptable
item.description: A teacher asks whether schools, very focused on detecting AI-generated work, explain clearly enough which uses are acceptable and how to declare them.

media:content.media:description: Diagram with the question “Which uses are allowed?” at the top. On the left, a document with a blue arrow leading to a scale, under the label “Declared process”. On the right, a document with an arrow leading to a red question mark, under the label “Hidden process”.

item.title: Cross-checking several AIs was a homemade trick; today Perplexity does it in a single query
item.description: In November 2025, the advice for trusting an answer was to ask two or three artificial intelligences and use another to look for the discrepancies. In February 2026, Perplexity turned that method into a feature.

media:content.media:description: Diptych split by a vertical line. On the left, “Nov. 2025”: three answers from three AIs that a person, drawn with head and shoulders and labelled “By hand”, compares. On the right, “Today”: the same three answers go into a single blue box with two zones, “Agree”, with a tick, and “Differ”.

item.title: Intelética, IBERAMIA’s open-access journal on artificial intelligence, ethics and society, accepts…
item.description: Intelética, IBERAMIA’s open-access journal on artificial intelligence, ethics and society, accepts articles in Spanish, Portuguese and English.

item.title: AI-text detectors are not proof, and institutions propose assessing the process instead
item.description: Programs that promise to reveal whether a piece of work was written by artificial intelligence get it wrong, including for students who have not used it, and even their own makers advise against punishing anyone on their say-so. This report explains what the studies, the European Regulation, data protection authorities and education guidelines say, and sets out a no-cost plan for assessing fairly in any subject: state which uses are allowed, ask for evidence of the process and listen to students.

media:content.media:description: Two-column infographic. On the left, under the label “Detector”, a document with a percentage bar and a question mark, and three warnings (an alert triangle, two speech bubbles and a half-and-half box) representing false positives, poorer results in a second language and failures with mixed texts; below, the label “Indication, not proof”. An arrow leads to the right, under the label “Process”, where four steps in a staircase labelled “Declared uses”, “Drafts”, “In stages” and “Oral explanation” lead to a person holding a scale and the label “A person decides”.

item.title: Gemini came and went in educational accounts; today the school switches it on or off
item.description: In November 2025, anyone using Gemini with an educational account could not tell which features they would find from one day to the next. A year later, Google has opened up features that were then denied to them, but for students’ accounts each school will decide.

media:content.media:description: Diptych split by a vertical line. On the left, “Nov. 2025”: two rows, “Gmail” with a video and a tick, and “XTEC” with a video and a red cross. On the right, “Today”: two school buildings, one with a switch turned on and the other with one turned off, next to the label “School”.

item.title: INTEF to present the 2026 update of its AI guide at SIMO on 13 November
item.description: According to INTEF’s programme at SIMO EDUCACIÓN, that day was to see the presentation of the new version of its guide on the use of AI in education and another on how to integrate it into schools.

media:content.media:description: A timeline under the label “13 November” with two sessions: at “10:30”, an open book labelled “AI guide”, and at “13:30”, a document labelled “Schools”.

item.title: Microsoft unveils Classroom, a dedicated space to centre classwork on Microsoft 365
item.description: Microsoft Classroom brings assignments, grades and AI tools together on a single screen for primary, secondary and higher education. It arrives in 2027 at no extra cost for schools on certain plans.

media:content.media:description: A panel labelled “Classroom” with four arrows leading to four boxes labelled “Tasks”, “Grades”, “Notebook” and “AI”.

item.title: England's university regulator calls for more assessment without AI and reopens the debate on how to verify authorship
item.description: The Office for Students recommends secure formats such as in-person or oral exams. In the group, members debated what can and cannot be detected.

media:content.media:description: A diagram in two halves: on the left, under the label “Secure formats”, three icons labelled “Oral” (a microphone), “Presentation” (a whiteboard) and “Practical” (a pencil); on the right, a magnifying glass crossed out in red with the label “Detector”.

item.title: UNESCO proposes five units for students aged 13 to 15 to question AI’s answers and decide for themselves
item.description: “AI answers. You decide” is a companion guide to UNESCO’s media and information literacy curriculum, with classroom discussions and activities that can be used separately.

media:content.media:description: A diagram of three concentric circles: “You” in the centre, “AI systems” around it and “People and institutions” in the outer ring; two curved arrows link the first two and a red arrow points from outside to the question “Where can I have a say?”. Below, the label “Five questions” and five boxes, one for each question in the guide.

item.title: England's university regulator clarifies which AI practices fit its quality conditions and publishes the study behind them
item.description: The Office for Students and Advance HE have put out a 48-page report, based on more than 300 students and staff, and a guide that translates its findings into registration conditions B1, B2 and B4.

media:content.media:description: Diagram from left to right: a document labelled “Report” leads to an open book labelled “Guide B1 B2 B4”, which forks into two assessment lanes: a closed padlock labelled “Closed” and an open padlock labelled “Open”.

item.title: The European AI literacy framework expected in December arrived in June, with the PISA 2029 assessment in the background
item.description: In November 2025, anyone looking for ways to teach critical thinking with artificial intelligence was pointed to a framework still in draft, with the final version announced for December. It arrived six months later.

media:content.media:description: Diptych split by a vertical line. On the left, labelled “Nov. 2025”: a text document, “Draft”, and below it an empty dotted box. On the right, labelled “Today”: the same document, now with a check mark, “Version 1.0”, and below it a filled box that reads “PISA 2029”.

item.title: Claude Whiteboards and Sheets, in beta, and Claude Data, which replaces Dashboards, were announced on 10…
item.description: Claude Whiteboards and Sheets, in beta, and Claude Data, which replaces Dashboards, were announced on 10 November and are available on all paid plans.

item.title: A second video with Fable 5.2 adds an agent that checks the scientific content before generating it
item.description: After the photosynthesis animation, the same teacher has made one on cellular respiration with a reviewing agent, and has translated the first into Catalan.

media:content.media:description: A chain of five steps with arrows, labelled “Script”, “Reviewer”, “Images”, “Reviewer” and “Video”, with a magnifying glass at each review step.

item.title: GPT-5.1 arrived in ChatGPT to amazement at its speed and did not last four months there
item.description: In November 2025, people were struck by how quickly GPT-5.1, OpenAI’s “more conversational” model, arrived. By 11 March 2026 it had already disappeared from ChatGPT.

media:content.media:description: Diptych split by a vertical line. On the left, labelled “Nov. 2025”, a chat bubble with lines of text and the label “GPT-5.1”. On the right, labelled “Today”, the same bubble but dashed and in blue, with the label “GPT-5.1” struck through and “Retired” below.

item.title: EduGems becomes EduPrompts because Google is replacing Gems with Skills
item.description: The site with 174 prompts for schools changes its name and address. The prompts can still be copied into any other AI tool.

media:content.media:description: At the top, a box labelled “EduGems” points to another labelled “EduPrompts”; below, a box “Gems” leads with a red arrow to another labelled “Skills”, and on the right a copy icon labelled “Copy”.

item.title: Gemini’s formulas reached Google Docs as code; a year on, Docs still does not understand LaTeX
item.description: In November 2025, Gemini was already writing and editing formulas in LaTeX, but when they were taken into Google Docs they arrived as code. A year on, Google’s word processor still cannot read LaTeX and the remedy is the same: an add-on or a separate editor.

media:content.media:description: Diptych split by a vertical line. On the left, “Nov. 2025”: a Google Docs page with the formula turned into code braces, labelled “Code”. On the right, “Today”: the same page with the same “Code”, and a blue arrow pointing to a blue puzzle piece labelled “Add-on”, the remedy that is still needed.

item.title: Someone who runs a Claude Code agent on their home NAS says it runs as a service with administrator…
item.description: Someone who runs a Claude Code agent on their home NAS says it runs as a service with administrator permissions, and that it asks before deleting data, touching disks or opening ports. It continues the thread on home automation with agents.

item.title: The website of the National Congress on Digitalisation in Education, held in Albacete on 5 and 6 November,…
item.description: The website of the National Congress on Digitalisation in Education, held in Albacete on 5 and 6 November, offers access to the broadcast of the talks, according to the group. (In Spanish.)

item.title: A group thread uses coding agents to control home automation
item.description: A thread in the group collects uses of agents such as Claude Code or Antigravity to run the television, music and the Home Assistant configuration, with control of privacy as a condition.

media:content.media:description: A diagram in which a box, “Agent”, points to a code document labelled “Configuration”, which points to a house labelled “Home Assistant”; below, a red padlock labelled “No passwords”.

item.title: The open model that was “checkmating” the giants: a year on, Kimi is almost three times bigger and still behind
item.description: In November 2025, people were sharing that a Chinese open-weights model, Kimi K2 Thinking, beat GPT-5 on some tests. Today Kimi K3, from the same family, is almost three times bigger, but its maker admits it does not match the best closed models.

item.title: An AI detector's percentage opens a conversation with the student, but does not prove they copied
item.description: A post on the blog “Familias con inteligencia” asks what to do when a detector flags the work of a student who says they wrote it themselves, and suggests backing the percentage up with evidence of the process.

media:content.media:description: A set of scales tipped to the right: on the lighter left pan, a card labelled “Detector 87%”; on the heavier right pan, another labelled “Drafts”, “Versions” and “Oral explanation”. Between the two pans, a magnifying glass and the label “A person decides”.

item.title: The BBC tested AI toys for young children: one of the soft toys replied “I can't help with killing you”…
item.description: The BBC tested AI toys for young children: one of the soft toys replied “I can't help with killing you” after misunderstanding a question. British MPs are asking retailers to withdraw these toys before Black Friday.

item.title: Juan José de Haro has expanded his article with the idea that different agents (Claude Code, Codex,…
item.description: Juan José de Haro has expanded his article with the idea that different agents (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity) can share a common body of knowledge that all of them can add to, as the paper reported on four-layer memory. It only works with agents installed on the computer, not with web versions.

item.title: The age for using AI in class depends on three different rules: those of the companies, the law and the education authorities
item.description: Each service’s terms, data protection law and some education authorities set different ages for using artificial intelligence, and they are often confused. This report explains what each says as of 6 November 2026, why research asks us to swap the question of age for the question of purpose, and how a primary or secondary teacher can decide which tool to use, with which account, and who operates it.

media:content.media:description: Infographic on an age ruler from 0 to 18, with marks at 13, 14 and 18, in three blocks. “Companies”: “OpenAI and Microsoft: from 13”, with a line from 13 to 18; “Anthropic: from 18”, with a dot at 18; and “Gemini with a school account: all ages”, with a bar from 0 to 18. “Data law”: “Own consent: from 14”, with a dashed line up to 14 and a solid one after it; and “At school, no consent needed: educational function”, with a bar from 0 to 18. “Some education authorities”: “Catalonia: the teacher operates the AI”, with a red line up to 14, and “From 14: inform, authorisation advisable”, with a line from 14; and “Basque Country: chatbots from 13”, with a cross before 13 and a line after it; and “Murcia: autonomous access from 3rd-year ESO”, with a dashed line up to 14 and a solid one after it. At the foot, “What for? Which account? Who operates it?”.

item.title: Anthropic proposes organising AI agents' memory into four layers with a periodic review
item.description: An Anthropic research text describes how to give an agent memory between sessions, and a teacher in the group has adapted their own system to that idea and explains it in an article with instructions.

media:content.media:description: Four stacked layers, from top to bottom labelled “Profile”, “Notes”, “Wiki” and “Conversations”, and a curved blue arrow rising from the conversations to the profile, next to a moon labelled “Night review”.

item.title: Teachers debate whether families’ authorisation is needed to use AI with students
item.description: One school has limited generative AI with its students because some families did not authorise it; other views hold that simply informing them is enough. The rules are clear: families must be informed, but between 14 and 18 their consent is not needed unless the tool requires it.

media:content.media:description: Infographic in two panels. On the left, “Under 14”, with a whiteboard and the label “In Catalonia, the teacher operates the AI”. On the right, “14 to 18”, with four rows: a megaphone, “Inform: always”; a pair of scales, “Consent: not needed”; a document with a tick, “Authorisation: advised in Catalonia”; and a document with a pencil, “Compulsory if the tool requires it”. Below, a band with a crossed-out person: “If a family objects, it only affects their child”.

item.title: Anthropic bans sustained, gratuitous abuse of its models in its usage policy
item.description: The update, published on 8 October 2026, takes effect on 12 November and will be enforced only in extreme cases.

media:content.media:description: A horizontal bar divided by a red line. On the left, labelled “Allowed”, three speech bubbles: two labelled “Frustration” and “Disagreement”. To the right of the line, a blue speech bubble labelled “Repeated cruelty” and, below it, a calendar labelled “From 12 Nov”.
